stories.body:
Chin-Wu Huang attended Miami University for about a year, from the fall of 1924 to the spring of 1925. Born in Shanghai, China, Huang was recommended to attend Miami by Professor C.H. Chuang at Tsing Hua College, who was also a former Miami student. Tsing Hua College was established as a school to prepare Chinese students whom the government wanted to send to the US. In the aftermath of the Boxer Rebellion and the granting of the Boxer Indemnity scholarship program, universities were a vital form of diplomacy. Though the Chinese Exclusion Act and Immigration Act of 1924 were both aimed at restricting emigration from China, education was seen as the loophole and a path to innovation and friendly relations. Huang and his brother, who attended Carleton College, were some of the few who were able to take advantage of that loophole and attend university in the US. 
Huang often showed sentiments of support and appreciation in his letters to President Hughes, grateful for his—albeit short—experience at Miami. He got involved on campus, including joining the Cosmopolitan Club, which worked to "promote intellectual relationships and friendships among the foreign and American students of the University." The club continued to promote these friendly relations even after Huang left. 
Education as a form of cultural exchange and diplomacy is best exemplified in the 1920s era of Chinese-American relations. While tensions ran high and the need to modernize in China was strong, seemingly trivial players in the great political game became the center of attention and unknowingly pawns of diplomacy. Universities in the US were placed at the center, where even President Hughes of Miami University became an important player, determining which class Huang and other Chinese students were to be placed into. Many students who came to Miami from China were previous graduates of Tsing Hua College, so it was up to the universities to decide if and how their credits transferred, even suggesting that admitting students to junior level standing would be too strenuous. In Huang's case, President Hughes corresponded with other universities to determine what the best course of action would be. After speaking with Williams College and Colorado College about the "Chinese Educational Mission," Hughes determined that Huang would be best placed in the junior level class. The increase in Chinese students to universities in the US was seen across the nation, from Ohio to Colorado. 
Continuing his education at Antioch College from 1925-1927, he kept in touch with the Miami president, going so far as to say “Since coming to Antioch, I am always thinking and yearning for Miami, a place that I never can find now so beautiful, so wholesome, and its people so kind.” At Antioch, Huang began to specify his major down to accounting. He worked at Ford Motor Company in Highlands Park, Michigan, where learned a myriad of skills, including “the way Americans manage the factory.” 
Huang’s appreciation and love for Miami and American culture could be viewed by the Chinese government as both a strength and a detriment. On one hand, he was gaining skills in the West to bring back to China, which was the point of the venture; on the other, he was becoming infatuated with the idea of America and American life, especially after attending Miami. 

Huang's story and time at Miami brings to the forefront the role of education as a split screen of both inclusion and exclusion. Chinese students would often form relations and stick together, as seen in the Cosmopolitan Club, but they also immersed themselves in American culture.  Ties to the US and Miami specifically for Huang lasted longer than his time there as a student: he sent gifts to Hughes when he was back in Shanghai, including tea. In a time of great tension on the international scale, education became the glue that held these relations together, a key example of diplomacy trickling down to the most local levels.

person.bio: Chin-Wu Huang was born in Shanghai, China and was a graduate of Tsing Hua College in Beijing. Now known as Tsinghua University, the college was established as a preparatory school after the Boxer Rebellion to help Chinese students study abroad in the United States. A high-achieving student, Huang was encouraged by Professor C.W. Chuang to study at Miami University. He arrived on campus on October 6, 1924 and entered as a junior. During his time at Miami, Huang was an active member of the Cosmopolitan Club, a student group focused on celebrating cultural diversity on campus. After receiving his bachelor’s degree, Huang continued his studies at Antioch College and later worked for the Ford Motor Company in Highland Parks, Michigan.

stories.body:
“Love is the divinist thing given to man.” – Ito, 1910, *Miami Student*

Chonosuke Ito was born on August 28, 1889 in Japan and immigrated to the United States in 1906. In 1909 he began coursework at Miami University in Ohio, where he was an active member of the student community. He published a couple of jokes within the Miami Student, joined Miami Union Literary Society in 1910, and gave many talks to the student body about his Japanese culture. In 1910, he gave a talk about schools and students in Japan. Later that year, Ito engaged with a fellow Japanese-born Miami student Kiyoshi Tomizawa in an exhibition/demonstration of Kendo, a Japanese style of fencing. All the while, Ito worked as an in-house private servant for Raymond Hughes, a professor in Chemistry, who would later become president of Miami University. Despite his active involvement in student life, there is only one picture of Ito which he sent to then President Raymond Hughes.  

After leaving Miami University in 1911, Ito was working in San Francisco, California as a traveling salesman with Banzai Trading Company by 1917. On his World War I registration card he requested exemption from the draft in order to retain his Japanese Citizenship. In 1920, he was living in Little Tokyo, the famed Japanese-American neighborhood of Los Angeles. He was living in a rooming house as a lodger alongside five other Japanese men, two Russians, one German and one Chinese man. At this time he remained a traveling salesman, even crossing the border on January 21, 1922 to Tijuana.
 
In the years following, Chonosuke wrote a letter to his former employer, now president, Raymond Hughes asking for a letter of recommendation. Ito described his time in Los Angeles as a “financial reverse.” He regretted that he might have to take up being a private servant again, since discriminatory practices barred Japanese from most other roles. Ito also expressed his resolve to return to Japan and the money earned in this role would be used for the journey.
 
Very little is known of Chonosuke’s life after this letter exchange in 1926. He did, however, remain in the United States and he returned to California, this time moving to San Francisco. His life, like so many others in the U.S., was drastically altered by the forced relocation and incarceration of people of Japanese descent during World War II.  At the time of his draft card filing, his mailing address was listed as the Santa Anita Assembly Center in Arcadia, City, now known as the Santa Anita Park. Opened as a racetrack on Christmas Day of 1934, the federal government seized control of the park from 1942-44 where it was used to host U. S. soldiers, imprison German soldiers of War, and then incarcerate 18,00-22,000 Japanese Americans.  Ito would later be temporarily incarcerated at Tule Lake Relocation Camp of California and indefinitely at Topaz Internment Camp in Delta, Utah.

Nothing more is known about his time after his release, presumably after the war. He died at the age of 61 on May 23, 1951 in San Joaquin County, California near Sacramento. Ito never married nor did he ever have children. While so much of his life after Miami was itinerant and a mystery, the humor, love for his Japanese culture, and fondness for connection with others remain as a legacy to his character despite the adversities he endured.

person.bio: Unlike many of his international student peers, Chonosuke Ito found his home in the United States. Graduating in 1910, Ito attempted to open a business in Los Angeles but moved to Chicago in 1920 after it failed. Deciding to go back to school, Ito contacted President Hughes with whom he shared a close relationship while he was an undergraduate to ask for a job reference. Hughes provided the recommendation and even offered Ito a job at Miami, reflecting the often close relationships between Asian students and faculty at Miami University.

stories.body:
Atsushi “Herbert” Saito was a Japanese American student who attended Miami University from 1940 to 1943. Born on April 21st, 1921 in Kapehu, Hawaii to parents Shinichi Saito and Onao Kurisu Saito, he grew up in North Hilo, Hawaii where both of his parents worked at a sugar cane plantation. Saito graduated from Hilo High School in 1939, spending a year working in the county clerk’s office before enrolling at Miami as a Liberal Arts major on a pre-law track in the fall of 1940.

During his time at Miami, Herbert was involved in a number of student organizations. He served as president of the Cosmopolitan Club— an international club that welcomed students of diverse backgrounds— and was a member of the Speakers Bureau, the Association of Miami Independents, Tau Kappa Alpha fraternity, and Les Politiques, a club for those interested in political science. Selected to participate in the Fisk Public Speaking Contest all three years he attended Miami, he placed third his freshman and sophomore years and second his senior year. Several of his speeches focused on his experiences growing up in the then-Hawaii Territory— in addition to public speaking opportunities, he also vocalized his support for Hawaiian statehood in publications like *The Miami Student*. When U.S. involvement in World War II created an increased need for Japanese translators, Saito volunteered to teach a non-credit Japanese course to assist his peers in learning the language. He taught the course for two years. He was one of many Miami students during the war years who, as part of a larger project conducted by history professor Dr. William E. Smith, documented both their daily campus lives and perceptions of the war through diary entries. Herbert graduated in the spring of 1943 and enlisted in the military that July, where he served as a linguist in the U.S. Army Air Force.

Following his return from war, Saito began teaching back home on Hilo, first at Kohala High School and then at Konawaena High School, where he would eventually retire from. An English teacher, he served as an advisor to a number of different extracurricular clubs, including the Kona Junior Rifle Club and the Kona Junior Young Buddhist Association. He married Ayoka “Ethel” Imai in 1950— the couple had three daughters together, Gloria, Darlene, and Jeanne. Herbert remained active in the Hilo community throughout his life, serving as a Sunday school teacher at his Honwanji Buddhist temple, commander of Post 20 of the American Legion, and secretary for the Kona Invitational Softball League.

Herbert Saito passed away on June 12th, 1993 at the age of seventy-two.

stories.body:
Kiyoshi Tomizawa was a Japanese American student who attended Miami University from 1908 to 1912. He was born on May 13th, 1879 in Fukushima, Japan to parents Seiga and Kame Tomizawa. Although Kiyoshi’s father was the minister of religion for the Sōma samurai clan during the Tokugawa Shogunate, the Tomizawa family lost much of its wealth and prestige when the Meiji Restoration of 1868 stripped daimyō feudal lords of their authority. Kiyoshi’s childhood was defined by economic insecurity— unable to afford the cost of raising three children, his father decided to send both him and his younger sister to be adopted by another family, the Kataokas, in 1890. Kiyoshi would return to the Tomizawa household in 1897 at the age of eighteen before moving to Sendai to attend Tohoku Gakuin University. It was there that he met Dr. John Raleigh Mott, founder of the World Student Christian Organization and later the head of the Y.M.C.A., a role for which he would win the 1946 Nobel Peace Prize. Inspired by Mott’s work, Tomizawa began to learn English and moved to San Francisco in November of 1903. He lived in the United States for a few years before enrolling at Miami University in the fall of 1908 to pursue a Liberal Arts degree.

Kiyoshi spent his first year on campus as a “special student” in the Academy, a Miami-run college prep program for high school students. Rather than residing in a dorm the following years, he stayed at the house of Professor Fred W. Stone. Involved in a number of student organizations, Tomizawa was a member of the gymnastics team, the Miami Union Literary Society, the Phrenocon Association (previously the non-Fraternity Association and later changing its name to Phi Kappa Tau, as it is known today), and the German club “Der Deutsche Verein”. He graduated in the spring of 1912, returning to Japan shortly after to teach English in Tokyo. It was there that he married Fumi Mezawa in 1913 before returning to the United States for permanent residency in 1914, settling down in San Francisco. The couple had four children together.

Tomizawa began working as an assistant secretary for the Japanese Chamber of Commerce upon his return to the United States. He was then hired as executive secretary for the Sutter Street Branch (also known as the Japanese Branch) of the San Francisco Y.M.C.A. upon its formation in 1918. For the next decade, Tomizawa worked tirelessly alongside other members of the Japanese American community of San Francisco to raise funds for a permanent home for the Japanese Branch. By the end of 1928, they had raised $40,000 in funds towards the purchase of a new building, received from donors in the United States and Japan alike. Thanks to these efforts, the location for the new Japanese Y.M.C.A. was purchased in March of 1929 and, after several financial setbacks due to the onset of the Great Depression, the building finally opened its doors in January of 1936. It is still operating today as the Buchanan Y.M.C.A.. In 1937, Tomizawa was honored by Miami University with the Bishop Medal, a recognition of his extraordinary career with the Japanese Y.M.C.A.. The Bishop Medal, established in 1936, is given to individuals who have distinguished themselves in service to humanity. The Bishop Medal is named after Robert Hamilton Bishop, Miami’s first president.
 
Though Kiyoshi retired from the Japanese Y.M.C.A. in 1939, the impact of his work on the Japan Town community continued long after his career at the Y ended, especially in the hearts and minds of the people he served. In 1942, Chojuro Numajiri, who worked at the Japanese Branch for twenty-three years, recalled working alongside Tomizawa: “I have yet to meet a more sincere Christian and a finer gentleman.” Troy Ishikawa, son of Roy Ishikawa, who lived at the Sutter Street Y.M.C.A. for a brief time in the 1930s, wrote a 2011 blog post in which he recalled Kiyoshi encouraging his father and other *kibei* (Japanese Americans born in the U.S. who, after being raised and educated in Japan, return to the states as an adult) to register to vote. As an *issei*, or first generation Japanese immigrant, Tomizawa was ineligible for citizenship and therefore could not vote, but wanted to ensure that the younger generation would give voice to Japanese American interests and problems facing their communities.

Following the attack on Pearl Harbor in 1941, Tomizawa, like many other Japanese Americans at the time, was investigated by the FBI for fear of potential espionage— a December 1941 FBI memo put him on a list of Japanese non-citizens to be considered for custodial detention. When Japanese internment began in 1942, he was given a choice: either join the hundreds of thousands of Japanese Americans forcibly relocated to internment camps, or serve the U.S. government as a Japanese instructor at the U.S. Navy Japanese Language School (soon renamed the Navy School of Oriental Languages) in Boulder, Colorado. Tomizawa chose the latter and began teaching Japanese to naval officers at the University of Colorado Boulder. He continued teaching at the Navy School of Oriental Languages into the 1950s before moving back to San Francisco to spend the rest of his retirement.

Kiyoshi Tomizawa passed away on August 5th, 1964 at the age of eighty-five.

stories.body:
H.R.H. Prasob (Ned) Mom Chow Suksvasti was a Siamese-American student at Miami University around 1934-1938. Born in Bangkok, Siam (Thailand), he came to the United States around 1927.

Sukhsvasti was not just an ordinary student: he was a member of Siamese royalty. In fact, the “H.R.H.” at the beginning of his name and “mom chow” in the middle indicates that he was a grandchild of the king. Siam in the early-mid 1930s was a land of political turmoil, with nationalism on the rise and financial instability running rampant. The influence of Western culture in Siam was significant, with many students going abroad to either Europe or the US to study. Sukhsvasti was sent to the US to attend Chestnut Hill Academy from 1928-1931. At the academy, he was a part of the soccer team, instrumental club, and class day committee. From Chestnut Hill he entered Princeton in 1931, a member of the class of 1935. Again heavily involved in student life, he was a prominent member of the wrestling team, tennis team, and “dramatics.” 

His time at Princeton was cut short, with a scandal that required him to transfer schools. Little is known about the events that unfolded on that fateful night of April 1933. All that was revealed to the  public was that the Campus Club was closed down. The press harassed Sukhsvasti and his team relentlessly. Local and national newspapers such as *Time*,*The New York Times*, *The Notre Dame Scholastic*, and *The Daily Princetonian* covered the story of his transfer. It was stated that Sukhsvasti simply got involved with the wrong crowd of people.

Interestingly enough, letters between Murray Sheehan, the liaison for the Siamese Legation, and Princeton's Dean Gauss indicated that Gauss actually heavily supported Sukhsvasti’s withdrawal from Princeton and in fact encouraged it, which is a different sentiment than indicated in the newspapers.

Restlessly, his liaison Muray Sheehan, himself a graduate of Miami, worked to protect Sukhsvasti’s integrity and, most importantly, his royal title. Sheehan reached out to multiple schools, including Miami University and William and Mary, to get Sukhsvasti placed in a good program.  

Sukhsvasti settled on Miami for his final destination. Dedicated to his academics, he was named to the dean’s list in September of 1933 and continued to remain invested in his education throughout his time at Miami. He shared his culture with Miami, often speaking at the church about Buddhism. An ardent member of the tennis team, he was always on the cusp of making varsity. 

However, back in Siam, a coup in 1932 had thrown the country into a sea of unknowns. Sukhsvasti was called back home. Reluctant to leave, the prince applied for relief in America, but was denied. Returning to Siam, he taught at a government school and worked at a newspaper. Finally, in 1937, he was allowed to return to the US to complete his degree. Back on campus, he became more involved than ever. He was a member of the national sociology honorary Alpha Kappa Delta, Sigma Chi, Cosmopolitan club, Peace Committee, Speaker’s Bureau, and Tennis Bureau. 

Students at Miami were just as excited as Sukhsvasti to have a prince on campus. Often featured in *The Miami Student*, he was a source of curiosity and cultural difference that other students were delighted to learn about. One article specifically details Siam dating culture and how it differs from the US. He explains that while Siam’s dating traditions are not as strict as China, they are more rigid than the US. His sentiments for the US is shown when he states that, “No country treats its women with the degree of equality shown here in America.”

On June 13, 1938, Sukhsvasti graduated from Miami with a degree in economics with honors. He married Princess Krishna on January 22, 1939 and had six children from 1940 to 1955. He worked for the Thai Government Service from 1938-46. From 1943-45 he was the Commercial and Financial Attache to the Royal Thai Embassy in Tokyo and was then the Economic Adviser to the Government Party from 1948-49 and came back to work as Thai Chief Delegate to ECAFE fourth session in Australia in 1948. He became an editor for the British Information Service. He published a multitude of works in the early 1940s including the *Handbook of Economic Principles* and the *Principles of Money* in 1941-42, as well as the *English Conversation Self-Taught*. In 1952, he was the president of the National Press Association in Thailand. Additionally, he was on the Board of Directors of the National Press Association of Thailand. 

In 1956, he made a speech at the Hague, recognizing Hungary’s calls for reform. He worked at the Thai diplomatic and civil service, as well as an editor in the Information of the British Embassy in Bangkok. His experience in the US and his comfortability with English allowed him to be able to translate English novels into Thai, also having written language and economic textbooks. Just as Sukhsvasti was heavily involved in college, he remained dedicated to being an active member in the community as he was a member of the American Universities Alumni Association, Old England Students Association, Royal Bangkok Sports Club, Royal Turf Club of Thailand, Reporters’ Club, and Royal Automobile Association of Thailand. He continued to play tennis and box. He passed away on August 12, 1985.

person.bio: Prasobsukh Sukhsvasti was a prince in the Thai royal family and represented one of the many Thai students who studied in the US during the 1930s. Students typically came from middle and upper class backgrounds and were expected to return to Thailand after their education abroad to help modernize the country. Sukhsvasti was the grandson of King Rama IV of Siam but during his time at Miami he preferred to be called “Ned.” Sukhsvasti hoped to use his Miami education to teach high school in Thailand or enter into the government bureaucracy.

stories.body:
Wing Kong Chong arrived at Miami University in the fall of 1938 on the University of Hawaii-Miami University Exchange Scholarship. Chong was born in Hilo, Hawaii on August 14th, 1916 to Charles Chong Man and En Fung Pung— his father was born in Canton, China and immigrated to the United States in the 1890s while his mother was born in Hawaii to Chinese parents. Wing Kong grew up in a neighborhood of Hilo known as “Chongville” after his father, who owned and operated the local meat market. After graduating from Hilo High School in 1936, he became enrolled at the University of Hawaii, spending two years as a student there before transferring to Miami through a foreign exchange program— as Hawaii was still considered a U.S. territory at the time— funded by the Miami University Chest Fund.

As a student at Miami, Chong studied education and was involved in various activities on campus. A member of both Tau Kappa Alpha, an honor society for public speaking, and the Speakers Bureau, he regularly gave speeches to local rotary clubs and community organizations about his experiences living in Hawaii. He was also a member of the Cosmopolitan Club, a student organization that welcomed students of diverse backgrounds, where he served as Sergeant at Arms. Though his exchange scholarship expired at the end of his junior year, Miami president Alfred Horatio Upham offered to waive his tuition for the 1939-1940 school year, praising Chong as “a fine young man who makes friends readily, and is the type we need rather badly, located as we are so far from either seaboard.” He graduated from Miami in the spring of 1940 before attending Columbia University for his master’s degree in education, graduating in 1941.

After moving back to Hawaii, Wing Kong taught at Mountain View Elementary, Hilo Intermediate School, and Hilo High School. He married Ethel Ishii in 1948— the couple had three children together, Curtis, Clayton, and Elisa. Chong became involved in politics in the 1960s, serving on the Board of Supervisors of Hawaii County from 1960 to 1962. He was elected to Hawaii’s House of Representatives from 1971 to 1974, and ran for mayor of Hawaii County in 1972 and 1974. In 1975, Chong was honored by Miami University with the Bishop Medal, in recognition of his extraordinary career as a teacher and public servant. The Bishop Medal, established in 1936, is given to individuals who have distinguished themselves in service to humanity. The Bishop Medal is named after Robert Hamilton Bishop, Miami’s first president.
 
Following his political career, Chong continued to work in the insurance business as an employee of American Mutual. He remained active in the Hilo community as a boy scout leader for over thirty years.

Wing Kong passed away April 25th, 2006, at the age of eighty-nine.
